drills.q: Name the three properties of a good North Star metric.
drills.a: Reflects real customer value (not company output), leads durable business value fast enough to steer by, and resists (but is never immune to) gaming.

drills.q: State Goodhart's Law in one sentence.
drills.a: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure -- people rationally optimize the metric itself once real incentives are tied to it, often decoupling it from the thing it was meant to proxy.

drills.q: A team's activation-rate leading indicator has hit target for three straight quarters but retention hasn't moved. What's the most likely explanation and how do you check it?
drills.a: The leading-to-lagging causal link has decayed or was correlational rather than causal to begin with, possibly because the activation definition drifted toward something easier once it became an explicit target (Goodhart). Re-validate the correlation on fresh cohort data and audit whether the underlying behavior satisfying the definition has shifted even if the formal definition hasn't changed.

drills.q: Why is a 3x increase in signups from a paid campaign potentially bad news, not good news?
drills.a: If Activation and Retention are unchanged, you've paid real CAC to acquire a larger cohort that behaves exactly like before -- this can actively worsen unit economics (payback period) rather than grow the business, since a wider funnel top doesn't help if the leak rate below it is unchanged.

drills.q: What makes a guardrail metric different from just tracking more dashboard metrics?
drills.a: A guardrail is designed against a SPECIFIC known cheap way to game the target metric, has a threshold and an owner, and ideally an automated check. A generic dashboard of many metrics with no such design gets diluted attention and doesn't reliably catch gaming.

drills.q: Give a real, named example of Goodhart's Law and explain the mechanism, not just the outcome.
drills.a: Wells Fargo, 2016: cross-sell targets tied to compensation. Employees rationally responded to the incentive by opening millions of unauthorized accounts -- the metric 'accounts opened' became the optimization target and decoupled entirely from genuine customer relationship depth, the thing it was meant to proxy.

drills.q: A VP proposes 'features shipped per quarter' as a team metric. How do you respond, and what do you propose instead?
drills.a: Name it explicitly as an output metric (measures company effort, not customer value) that incentivizes shipping more, smaller, less-validated work. Propose an outcome-oriented leading indicator tied to the team's actual North Star instead; if a faster cadence is needed, offer a leading indicator of adoption/value (e.g. two-week adoption rate of shipped features) rather than reverting to a pure count.

drills.q: Design a North Star and at least two guardrails for an AI coding assistant feature.
drills.a: North Star: accepted-suggestion rate that survives to a shipped, largely-unmodified commit within N days (proxies real value, not just a shown/clicked suggestion). Guardrails: bug/regression rate attributable to AI-suggested code (catches fast-but-wrong acceptance), and a quarterly manual review of a sample of accepted suggestions for real usefulness vs. rubber-stamped acceptance (catches suggestions trending toward bland/boilerplate to inflate acceptance rate without raising real value).

drills.q: Why does the intensity of Goodhart mitigation (guardrails, qualitative review) need to scale with how long a metric has been an incentive target, rather than being applied uniformly everywhere?
drills.a: Goodhart's effect compounds with how directly and how long a metric has been tied to real incentives (compensation, promotion) -- a brand-new internal dashboard number has little gaming pressure on it yet, while a metric that's driven bonuses for multiple quarters has had sustained rational optimization pressure applied against it. Uniform, heavy mitigation everywhere wastes effort; targeted mitigation on long-tenured incentive metrics catches the real risk.
